newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler U.S. June vehicle sales fall 4 percent.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler U.S. June vehicle sales fall 4 percent.

text.p: Leaning heavily on incentives, Chrysler Corp. on Tuesday reported a 4 percent decline in June U.S. light vehicle sales from a year ago, a smaller drop than analysts had expected.
Japanese automakers, which have been stealing market share from Detroit's Big Three all year, posted mixed U.S. results.
Chrysler, the U.S. No. 3 automaker said it sold 219,756 vehicles in the month, compared with 228,828 for June 1996. Chrysler said the figures represent its third best June in company history.
Among Japanese carmakers, Toyota Motor Corp. said sales fell 2.3 percent for the month to 96,040 units. But they were up 9.7 percent to 629,238 units for the first six months of 1997, a new record.

Honda Motor Co. Ltd., riding strong sales of its Civic small car and CR-V small sport utility vehicle, posted an 8.9 percent increase in June to 79,382 units. Nissan Motor Co. Ltd., said its sales rose 2.4 percent to 66,705.

At Chrysler, passenger car sales fell 14 percent to 72,480 units. Light trucks, including pickup trucks, minivans and sport utilities, rose 2 percent to 147,276. Combined minivan sales, spurred by increased incentives ranging from $750 to $1,000, rose 2 percent to their best finish so far this year.
While cars were weak as forecast, analysts had expected light trucks to fall around 5 percent, contributing to a total decline of 10 percent. Instead, they surged forward at the end of the month.
"It's the trucks that really carried the mail," said Lehman Brothers analyst Joseph Phillippi.

Chrysler's Grand Cherokee and Cherokee sport utility vehicles had sales of 22,728 and 14,062, increases of 2 percent and 3 percent, respectively. Grand Cherokee sales were aided by dealer incentives and low financing rates.

Chrysler officials noted vehicles that were not involved in sales incentive programs, such as the Dodge Dakota compact pickup truck, also did well. The Dakota had sales of 11,622, a 61 percent increase from a production-constrained 7,223 a year ago. The Dodge Ram full-size pickup also showed signs of reversing a May sales plunge with sales of 29,912, a drop of 5 percent.
"The non-incentive part of the lineup has led this month's strong sales results as much as anything else," said Steve Torok, executive director of sales and marketing operations.

However, Chrysler does not plan to let up on rebates and other incentives. Torok said the automaker extended until July 15 dealer incentives on the Grand Cherokee and many car lines, as well as rebates on its minivans.
"We want to see a little bit where the rest of the industry is at before we redo any of our programs," he said.

Chrysler included one milestone in its June results: the first four official sales of its much-awaited Prowler roadster. Torok said the cars were internal sales and will be used for advertising and promotional functions. He said the first retail sales will come later in July.

Among other automakers reporting Tuesday, Mitsubishi Motors Corp., said its June sales tumbled 31 percent to 13,751. Isuzu Motor Co. Ltd. reported a 5 percent sales decline to 9,126. Subaru of America Inc., a unit of Fuji Heavy Industries Ltd reported a U.S. June sales increase of 17 percent to 10,329 units.
General Motors Corp. is scheduled to report sales Wednesday, followed by Ford Motor Co. Thursday.
